1: # Framer — Capsid–receptor mapping on BMECs as a determinant of AAV transcytosis vs. intracellular retention
2: 
3: **Question under framing:** *Can molecular mapping of AAV capsid–receptor interactions on brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) determine which AAV variants transcytose across the blood–brain barrier versus remain intracellular, and for which capsid–receptor binding signatures?*
4: 
5: I will not answer until the problem is defined and worked through. Structure: (0) fix the terms; (1) relay current understanding; (2) state predictions; (3) decompose the causal problem; (4) analyze; (5) locate where parallel compute would and would not matter; (6) verdict.
6: 
7: ---
8: 
9: ## 0. Definitions and scope — what the question is actually asking
10: 
11: **0.1 "Molecular mapping of capsid–receptor interactions on BMECs."**
12: I read this as a *binding map*: a table of (capsid variant) × (BMEC surface molecule) entries with molecular resolution — receptor identity, binding site/epitope, affinity and kinetics (k_a, k_d, K_D), stoichiometry/avidity, glycan-versus-protein dependence, pH-sensitivity, and ideally structure. Technologies that produce such maps today include unbiased human membrane-proteome/secretome cell microarrays, which can assay more than 90% of the known human membrane proteome and secretome (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-52149-0); receptor pull-down selections coupled to NGS (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8); surface plasmon resonance and bio-layer interferometry of purified ectodomains (ALPL–capsid K_D ≈ 20 nM at pH 7.4 measured by SPR: https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9; TfR1–capsid kinetics by BLI: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769326); glycan arrays (used to identify AAVrh.10 sulfated LacNAc binding: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8577363); genetic loss-of-function screens (AAVR discovery by haploid genetic screen: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26814968); and structural mapping by cryo-EM of capsids (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7UD4) plus cryo-electron tomography and AlphaFold-Multimer models of capsid–interactor complexes (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518).
13: 
14: **0.2 "Transcytose versus remain intracellular."**
15: The outcome of interest is apical-to-basolateral passage of an intact, still-functional particle across a polarized BMEC layer, as measured in primary human brain microvascular endothelial cell transwell models (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27718541). This must be kept distinct from at least four other fates of an internalized particle: (i) *endothelial transduction* — nuclear delivery and transgene expression in the BMEC itself (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jnc.13898); (ii) *apical recycling* back to blood; (iii) *retrograde traffic* to the trans-Golgi network (the canonical productive route for AAV transduction: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391/); and (iv) *lysosomal degradation*. Brain endothelial cells route internalized cargo between recycling, retrograde/TGN, and lysosomal destinations (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12987-019-0134-9; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363266/), and lysosomal degradation is the dominant fate for most macromolecules taken up by these cells (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12987-019-0134-9). "Remain intracellular" in the question is therefore a *class* of fates (retention + degradation + TGN-diverted transduction), not one thing.
16: 
17: **0.3 "Determine" — the operative verb.**
18: Two readings, which I will answer separately in §4:
19: - **(D-sufficiency)** Is the binding map a *sufficient statistic* for fate, such that knowing the map fixes the classification of each variant?
20: - **(D-practical)** Can a classifier built on binding-derived features be made accurate enough to be *useful* (e.g., to prioritize variants, or to declare a signature class)?
21: 
22: **0.4 "Binding signatures."**
23: The multivariate pattern of binding features — receptor identity and topology, epitope geometry relative to the natural ligand, kinetic regime (especially pH-resolved off-rate), avidity/valency regime, glycan class, and the capsid context in which the binding element is presented — that co-occurs with a fate.
24: 
25: **0.5 Made precise, the question is:** is there a function *f*: binding-signature → {transcytose, retain} that is (i) derivable from molecular binding data and (ii) accurate; and if so, what does its domain (the set of signatures for which *f* is trustworthy) look like?
26: 
27: ---
28: 
29: ## 1. Current understanding (relayed before any analysis)
30: 
31: ### 1.1 What physically must happen
32: 
33: Systemic AAV penetration into brain parenchyma involves three steps: receptor binding at the brain endothelial cell surface, receptor-mediated internalization, and transcytosis to the brain parenchyma (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8). The BBB is formed mainly by BMECs joined by tight junctions, together with pericytes and astrocytic end-feet, and restricts passage of large molecules including AAV particles (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205). Brain endothelial cells uniquely both form tight junctions and *actively suppress* transcellular vesicle trafficking relative to peripheral endothelia (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12024798). Transcytosis is classically partitioned into receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) and non-selective adsorptive transcytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12024798), and the receptors involved include insulin receptor, transferrin receptor and LDL receptor family members (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804).
34: 
35: ### 1.2 The known capsid–receptor pairs relevant to BMECs
36: 
37: - **AAVR (KIAA0319L)** is an essential, broadly required AAV entry receptor identified by an unbiased haploid genetic screen, and it rapidly endocytoses from the plasma membrane and traffics to the trans-Golgi network (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26814968). Different serotypes engage different AAVR ectodomain polylactosamine/protein-doughnut (PKD) domains — AAV5 primarily via PKD1, AAV2 via PKD2, AAV1 and AAV8 via a combination (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00391-17). Cell-surface attachment is AAVR-independent and AAVR engagement may occur after endocytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391/).
38: - **Glycan attachment.** AAV9 uses terminal N-linked galactose as its primary receptor (https://www.jci.org/articles/view/57367), with the galactose-binding pocket mapped to N470, D271, N272, Y446 and W503 at the base of the three-fold protrusions (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12); N272A and W503A abolish galactose-dependent transduction (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.00448-12), and intact galactose binding has been reported to be important for BBB crossing and brain transduction (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13462111). AAVrh.10 binds sulfated LacNAc/keratan sulfate at a pocket equivalent to the AAV9 galactose site and can also use terminal galactose (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8577363). Heparan sulfate proteoglycan is used by AAV2, AAV3, AAV6 and AAV13, and sialic acid by AAV1, AAV4, AAV5 and AAV6 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8577363).
39: - **Mouse BBB: LY6A (SCA-1).** AAV-PHP.B/PHP.eB cross the mouse BBB by binding the GPI-anchored protein LY6A on brain endothelial cells (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0225206). LY6A expression on brain microvasculature is strain-dependent (high in C57BL/6J, substantially reduced in BALB/cJ), which is what made the receptor identifiable (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463). Ectopic LY6A expression raises PHP.eB binding/transduction ≥30-fold even in cells lacking galactose and AAVR (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855452). Whether LY6A engagement is *sufficient* for transcytosis, or whether transcytosis still depends on AAVR, was explicitly left unresolved (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855452). A related protein, LY6C1, can be co-opted by engineered inserts and works across both mouse strains (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112).
40: - **Human/primate-conserved RMT receptors engaged by engineered capsids.**
41:   - *TfR1*: BI-hTFR1, an AAV9-based 7-mer insert variant, binds human transferrin receptor and is actively transported across human brain endothelial cells, giving 40–50× greater CNS reporter expression than AAV9 in human TFRC knock-in mice, with the gain absent in wild-type mice (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386). It binds the apical domain of TfR1 at a site distinct from transferrin, so it does not compete with the natural ligand (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240104444092/en/Apertura-Gene-Therapy-Unveils-Novel-Engineered-AAV-Capsids-Targeting-Human-Transferrin-Receptor-1-for-Neurological-Gene-Therapy-Delivery).
42:   - *LRP6*: an unbiased human cell-surface interactome screen identified LRP6 as the BBB transcytosis receptor used by AAV9-X1.1 and AAV.CAP-Mac; the VR-VIII inserted peptides bind LRP6 YWTD domains 1–2, and LRP6 is highly conserved in humans (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-52149-0).
43:   - *CA-IV (CA4)*: variants 9P31/9P36 use the primate-conserved GPI-linked enzyme carbonic anhydrase IV, expressed on the luminal surface of brain endothelium (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205); engineered AAV-hCA4-IV77 gives ~100-fold greater brain transduction than AAV9 in mice expressing human CA-IV (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8).
44:   - *ALPL*: the TRACER-evolved capsid VCAP-102 uses tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase as its primary receptor; direct binding triggers receptor-mediated transcytosis in a cell-barrier model, the complex dissociates rapidly at pH 5.5 (consistent with basolateral release after endosomal acidification), and ALPL inhibition blocks transcytosis (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9).
45: - **Species restriction is the rule, not the exception.** Nearly all published mouse BBB-crossing AAV capsids act through LY6A or LY6C1, which are not present in primates (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112); LY6A is absent from primate endothelium (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8370029). AAV-BR1 (insert NRGTEWD) targets brain endothelium in mice but not in Sprague-Dawley rats (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41434-025-00563-4).
46: 
47: ### 1.3 Documented dissociations between binding and transcytosis (the core of my prior)
48: 
49: - **Crossing without transducing.** In primary human BMVEC transwells, AAV9 penetrates the barrier more effectively than AAV2 while *transducing the endothelium less well*; AAV9 crosses by an active, cell-mediated process without disrupting TEER, tight-junction proteins or inflammatory status (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27718541; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820). The accompanying editorial highlights the inverse relationship: AAV9 shuttles across BMVECs with minimal BMVEC transduction, whereas AAV2 is blocked and instead transduces the endothelium (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jnc.13898).
50: - **Binding ≠ transport in vivo.** In the TRACER screen, correlation between capsid performance and mouse brain microvascular endothelial cell binding was limited to one unique sequence group; the authors conclude monolayer BMVEC cultures are a poor predictor of in vivo transport across the BBB (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7841218).
51: - **In vitro rank ≠ in vivo rank.** In the CA-IV campaign, two top-performing capsids in "humanized" mice ranked relatively low in the in vitro selection and outperformed several top-ranked in vitro candidates (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8).
52: - **Same capsid, same receptor, opposite fate.** AAV9-X1.1 targets LRP6 in both rodents and primates, yet in rodents it primarily transduces endothelial cells rather than crossing, while in neonatal non-human primates the same capsid–receptor pair yields productive transcytosis and neuronal targeting (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8).
53: - **Sorting, not binding, decides fate.** For transferrin-receptor cargos, high-affinity or bivalent binding prevents transcytosis and drives lysosomal delivery, whereas monovalent/low-affinity formats are sorted for transcytosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804). A monovalent TfR Brain Shuttle construct localizes to intracellular sorting tubules and transcytoses, while a bivalent construct clusters, fails to enter tubules and is degraded; forcing tubule entry via Rab17 overexpression is sufficient to convert the degradative construct into a transcytosing one (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2). Endosomal tubular sorting networks route cargo away from lysosomes toward recycling, MVB or TGN destinations (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363266/).
54: - **"Signature" is capsid-contextual, not a portable motif.** Transferring the PHP.B 7-mer insert from AAV9 to AAV1 does not transfer Ly6a binding; a contiguous interface between the insert and surrounding HVR-VIII residues is required (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.01164-21). A PHP.B insert in an AAV5 backbone is not sufficient for the particle to cross the endothelial barrier, leading to the proposal that the insert facilitates endothelial engagement while another co-receptor enables apical-to-basolateral trafficking of the AAV9 context (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8370029).
55: - **One structural feature can move two receptor interactions in opposite directions.** The 2.24 Å cryo-EM structure of PHP.eB shows the 7-mer loop adopts a bent conformation set by engineered lysine–aspartate contacts; loop topology tracks AAVR-PKD2 binding strength, and PHP.eB simultaneously gains LY6A binding and weakens AAVR engagement (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7UD4; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9382559).
56: 
57: ### 1.4 Assays and model systems in use
58: 
59: Primary human BMVEC transwells (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27718541); hCMEC/D3 + primary astrocytes + iPSC-derived cortical neuron tri-cultures with barcoded capsid-shuffled libraries and a siRNA screen that identified genes affecting AAV transcytosis (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/methods/fulltext/S2329-0501(22)00127-9); MDCK cells engineered to overexpress ALPL, in which VCAP-102 transcytoses efficiently while parental AAV9 does not and parental MDCK cells support neither (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf); "humanized" mice expressing a human receptor in brain endothelium for in vivo transcytosis-based selection (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8); RNA-driven (TRACER) and Cre-based (CREATE) directed-evolution platforms (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7841218; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205); and machine-learning sequence-to-function atlases such as Fit4Function, whose models trained on mouse in vivo and human in vitro data predicted macaque biodistribution (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50555-y), alongside ML-guided capsid engineering generally (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-00793-4).
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ## 2. Predictions (stated before analysis)
64: 
65: - **P1 — Asymmetry of exclusion vs. confirmation.** A binding map will be good at *ruling out* (a capsid that binds nothing on BMECs will not transcytose) and weak at *ruling in*. I predict no complete overlap of signatures with transcytosis competence.
66: - **P2 — Affinity alone will not discriminate.** The fate-discriminating features will be kinetics and avidity regime (including pH-resolved off-rate), not K_D at a single pH or a single equilibrium measurement.
67: - **P3 — Receptor topology will be predictive.** GPI-anchored, raft-associated engagement (LY6A/LY6C1 in mouse; CA-IV in primate/human) will form one signature class; transmembrane RMT receptors engaged at apical epitopes away from the natural ligand site (TfR1 apical domain, LRP6 YWTD E1E2, ALPL) will form another. Both will be enriched for transcytosis; neither will be sufficient.
68: - **P4 — Avidity will be non-monotonic.** Signatures implying strong multivalent clustering of a transmembrane receptor will be *anti*-predictive of transcytosis and pro-predictive of lysosomal routing, by analogy with the TfR affinity/valence rules.
69: - **P5 — Glycan-only signatures will be pro-retention.** Attachment signatures dominated by galactose/sialic acid/HSPG without a protein RMT partner will correlate with endothelial transduction or intracellular handling rather than transcytosis (with AAV9 as the instructive exception that shows the map is incomplete).
70: - **P6 — Irreducible false positives.** Any classifier derived from binding data alone will have false positives that can only be removed by functional transcytosis readouts; I predict the residual error is not computable away.
71: - **P7 — Mouse signatures will not translate.** Signatures derived from LY6A/LY6C1 will fail in human BMECs.
72: - **P8 — The highest-value single addition to a binding map** will be a pH-resolved kinetic profile (on-rate at pH 7.4, off-rate at pH 7.4 vs. pH 5.5–6.0), because basolateral release after endosomal acidification is a documented mechanism (ALPL–VCAP-102: https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9).
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 3. Problem decomposition
77: 
78: **3.1 The causal chain, with the mapping's purchase points.**
79: 
80: `blood encounter → apical attachment (glycan + protein) → receptor engagement → internalization route (clathrin / caveolae / CLIC-GEEC / macropinocytosis) → endosomal sorting decision → {transcytotic tubule & basolateral release | apical recycling | retrograde/TGN → nuclear import → endothelial transduction | lysosome}`
81: 
82: A binding map covers only the first three links. The literature says the fate decision is made at link 5: brain endothelial cells route internalized cargo between recycling, TGN and lysosomal fates (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12987-019-0134-9), and transcytosis-competent cargos must avoid the lysosomal network that otherwise captures most macromolecules (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12987-019-0134-9; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363266/).
83: 
84: **3.2 What a binding map does capture.** Receptor identity and topology; epitope/steric relationship to natural ligands; affinity and kinetics, including pH-sensitivity; avidity/valency; glycan class; capsid-context presentation (loop topology, insert geometry); species orthology of the receptor; competition with endogenous ligands.
85: 
86: **3.3 What it does not capture (latent variables).** Which endosomal subdomain the receptor–ligand complex partitions into (early endosome vs. late endosome/lysosome vs. sorting tubule); Rab/retromer/tubule machinery engagement (Rab17 overexpression alone can flip a degradative construct to transcytosing: https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2); receptor recycling rate and polarized recycling destination; cell-state and species-specific expression (LY6A strain restriction: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463); glycocalyx shielding; hemodynamic and shear effects; pericyte/astrocyte induction of BBB phenotype; and the post-endocytic requirement for AAVR in productive infection vs. mere passage (AAVR's role in entry is established, but whether LY6A-mediated passage is AAVR-independent was left open: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6855452; AAVR engagement may occur after endocytosis: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8413391/).
87: 
88: **3.4 The mapping problem, split.**
89: (a) *Coverage*: which (capsid, receptor) pairs bind at all — solvable by high-throughput interactome mapping.
90: (b) *Signature → fate*: the classification problem posed by the question — this is where sufficiency is in doubt.
91: (c) *Generalization across species and cell states* — where most published signatures break.
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. Analysis
96: 
97: ### 4.1 (D-sufficiency) Is the binding map a sufficient statistic for fate? No.
98: 
99: Three independent lines of counterexample, any one of which breaks sufficiency:
100: 
101: 1. **Same map, different fate.** AAV9-X1.1 engages LRP6 in both rodents and primates, yet primarily transduces endothelial cells in rodents while transcytosing and targeting neurons in neonatal NHPs (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8). A binding map of AAV9-X1.1 on BMEC LRP6 is identical in the two cases; the fates differ.
102: 2. **Binding rank does not transport.** Monolayer BMVEC binding predicted in vivo BBB transport for only one sequence group (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7841218); top in vitro CA-IV binders were outperformed in vivo by lower-ranked variants (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8).
103: 3. **Fate is set by sorting, not attachment.** Bivalent/high-affinity TfR engagement drives lysosomes while monovalent/low-affinity engagement transcytoses, and Rab17-driven tubule entry can convert the former into the latter (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2). A static binding signature does not encode the tubule-entry propensity it induces.
104: 
105: Additionally, the object being mapped is context-dependent: the PHP.B 7-mer does not transfer Ly6a binding from AAV9 to AAV1 without its flanking HVR-VIII interface (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.01164-21), and in an AAV5 backbone the same insert does not confer endothelial crossing (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8370029). A "signature" recorded as a portable peptide motif is therefore not a stable object; it must be recorded as a capsid-contextual surface.
106: 
107: **Conclusion (D-sufficiency):** the binding map is *necessary but not sufficient*. It cannot by itself determine transcytosis vs. intracellular retention.
108: 
109: ### 4.2 (D-practical) Is the map informative? Yes — asymmetrically.
110: 
111: - **Exclusion works.** Non-binders fail: AAV2, which does not appreciably cross or transduce brain endothelium in vivo, is out-penetrated by AAV9 in human BMVEC transwells (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27718541); parental AAV9 does not transcytose in the MDCK-ALPL model while VCAP-102 does (https://www.voyagertherapeutics.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/POSTER-Voyager_ASGCT_2024_FINAL_Ishan.pdf).
112: - **Receptor-class signatures carry real signal.** Capsids engineered to bind LY6A or LY6C1 are strongly enriched for mouse brain transduction in a strain- and expression-dependent way (https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112); capsids with the LRP6-binding VR-VIII peptide class show conserved BBB-crossing behavior in NHPs (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-52149-0); the TfR1 apical-epitope class gives receptor-dependent, actively transported brain delivery (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386); the ALPL class shows pH-dependent release consistent with basolateral discharge (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9).
113: - **The field has converged on a "target-a-receptor" design grammar**, i.e., binding maps are already being used prospectively to generate transcytosis-competent capsids (receptor-targeted engineering against LY6A/LY6C1, TfR1, CA-IV, ALPL: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8; https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9) — which is evidence that the map is *actionable* even though it is not *decisive*.
114: 
115: ### 4.3 The binding-signature classes that survive the evidence
116: 
117: Predictions P3, P4, P8 survive; P2 survives in refined form (kinetics + pH-resolved off-rate matter more than equilibrium K_D); P5 needs qualification (AAV9's galactose engagement is reported to be important for BBB crossing, so glycan attachment is not purely pro-retention — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13462111 — but glycan-only classes still lack a demonstrated RMT mechanism).
118: 
119: A signature class *S* is **transcytosis-competent** to the degree it has:
120: 
121: 1. **A receptor that is (i) expressed on the luminal/apical surface of BMECs and (ii) known or plausible to enter RMT routes** — e.g., TfR1 (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386), LRP6 (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-52149-0), CA-IV (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10975205), ALPL (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9), or a GPI-anchored raft protein (LY6A/LY6C1 in mouse: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; CA-IV in human).
122: 2. **An epitope that does not compete with the natural ligand** (BI-hTFR1 binds the apical TfR1 domain away from the transferrin site: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240104444092/en/Apertura-Gene-Therapy-Unveils-Novel-Engineered-AAV-Capsids-Targeting-Human-Transferrin-Receptor-1-for-Neurological-Gene-Therapy-Delivery) and that is presented on an accessible capsid surface given the *specific* capsid loop context (https://journals.asm.org/doi/10.1128/jvi.01164-21).
123: 3. **A pH-resolved kinetic profile consistent with capture at pH 7.4 and release at endosomal pH** (rapid ALPL–VCAP-102 dissociation at pH 5.5: https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9).
124: 4. **An avidity regime in the permissive window** — enough to trigger internalization, not so multivalent/clustered as to be sorted to lysosomes (TfR valence/affinity rules: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2).
125: 5. **Species-matched receptor orthology and expression** (LY6A absent from primate endothelium: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8370029; LY6A/LY6C1 not present in primates: https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112; AAV-BR1 fails in rats: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41434-025-00563-4).
126: 
127: A signature class is **pro-retention / pro-endothelial-transduction** when it is dominated by attachment glycans without an RMT partner (AAV2-like HSPG handling: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820), or when it implies high-avidity clustering of a transmembrane receptor (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804), or when the receptor's default routing in that species is degradative.
128: 
129: ### 4.4 Answer
130: 
131: **Can molecular mapping determine transcytosis vs. intracellular retention?** Not in the sufficiency sense. The binding map is a *necessary, high-value, asymmetric* classifier: excellent for exclusion and for enriching priors by receptor class, incapable of fixing fate, because the fate decision is made by post-endocytic sorting machinery and by species/cell-state variables that are not functions of the capsid–receptor complex alone. The documented same-signature/different-fate case of AAV9-X1.1 (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8) is the cleanest single disproof.
132: 
133: **For which binding signatures does mapping get closest to determinative?** For signatures that specify *receptor class + epitope geometry + pH-resolved kinetics + avidity regime + capsid context*, and that are evaluated in a species-matched system. Concretely: apical, non-ligand-competing engagement of a conserved RMT receptor (TfR1 apical domain, LRP6 YWTD E1E2, ALPL, CA-IV) with a pH-sensitive off-rate and moderate avidity, presented by the specific capsid loop context in which it was selected — this class is enriched for transcytosis. GPI-anchored LY6A/LY6C1 engagement is a *mouse-only* transcytosis signature (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6520463; https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pbio.3002112). Glycan-attachment-only signatures and high-avidity clustering signatures are pro-retention (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6513804). Even in the best class, the map's residuals must be resolved by functional transcytosis assays (transwell flux, humanized-receptor in vivo selection), which is exactly the practice the field has adopted (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/methods/fulltext/S2329-0501(22)00127-9; https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(25)01190-8).
134: 
135: **Answer in one sentence:** molecular mapping can *partition* the space and *enrich* for transcytosis-competent capsid–receptor signatures, and can *exclude* non-binders, but it cannot *determine* fate, and the signatures where it is nearly determinative are the ones that add pH-resolved kinetics, epitope topology, avidity regime and capsid context to receptor identity.
136: 
137: ---
138: 
139: ## 5. Where more parallel compute would and would not change this
140: 
141: **Would not change:** the sufficiency conclusion. The disproofs are experimental (AAV9-X1.1 species divergence; BMVEC binding vs. in vivo transport; TfR valence sorting), and the latent variables are cellular, not computational. No amount of simulation of capsid–receptor complexes yields the Rab17/tubule partition of a complex in a polarized human BMEC (https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2).
142: 
143: **Could change (in degree, not in kind):**
144: 1. **Structural/biophysical coverage of the signature space.** Exhaustive AlphaFold-Multimer/cryo-ET/MD modeling of capsid–receptor–glycan complexes across thousands of variants and receptors, at multiple pH values, could turn "epitope geometry and pH-resolved kinetics" from a per-complex experiment into a computed prior (methods precedent: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11381518; https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7UD4).
145: 2. **Sequence-to-function models over capsid space.** Fit4Function-style ML trained on paired binding *and* transcytosis labels could compress the 7-mer/12-mer insert space and design multi-trait libraries with lower false-positive rates (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-50555-y; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40176349).
146: 3. **Kinetic/stochastic models of endosomal sorting.** Parallel simulation of receptor–cargo–endosome partitioning (recycling vs. tubule vs. lysosome) parameterized by measured affinities and valences could predict the P4 non-monotonic avidity window without exhaustive transwell assays (framework: https://www.cell.com/cell-reports/fulltext/S2211-1247(17)31707-2; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12363266/).
147: 
148: ---
149: 
150: ## 6. Verdict
151: 
152: The question is answerable now by reasoning over existing evidence: binding is necessary but not sufficient; fate is decided by post-endocytic sorting and species/cell-state context; and the near-determinative signatures are identifiable as a class (apical, non-competing RMT-receptor epitopes with pH-sensitive release and permissive avidity, in the correct capsid context). The binding constraint is experimental measurement of intracellular sorting fates and human-relevant transcytosis, not computation.
153: 
154: VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

## Abstract

Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) are foundational gene delivery tools for basic science and clinical therapeutics. However, lack of mechanistic insight, especially for engineered vectors created by directed evolution, can hamper their application. Here, we adapt an unbiased human cell microarray platform to determine the extracellular and cell surface interactomes of natural and engineered AAVs. We identify a naturally-evolved and serotype-specific interaction between the AAV9 capsid and human interleukin 3 (IL3), with possible roles in host immune modulation, as well as lab-evolved low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 6 (LRP6) interactions specific to engineered capsids with enhanced blood-brain barrier crossing in non-human primates after intravenous administration. The unbiased cell microarray screening approach also allows us to identify off-target tissue binding interactions of engineered brain-enriched AAV capsids that may inform vectors’ peripheral organ tropism and side effects. Our cryo-electron tomography and AlphaFold modeling of capsid-interactor complexes reveal LRP6 and IL3 binding sites. These results allow confident application of engineered AAVs in diverse organisms and unlock future target-informed engineering of improved viral and non-viral vectors for non-invasive therapeutic delivery to the brain.

**Subject terms:** Blood-brain barrier, Genetic vectors, High-throughput screening, Cryoelectron tomography

Engineered adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) aim to improve safety and potency for use in gene therapy but mechanisms underlying these features are poorly understood. Here, authors use unbiased screens to identify an interaction with the human immune system and a determinant of enhanced brain potency.

## Introduction

Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) have become the gene delivery vector of choice at the bench and in the clinic[1](#CR1),[2](#CR2). Systemic administration of AAVs, such as AAV9[3](#CR3)–[6](#CR6), allows noninvasive gene delivery, particularly in large or distributed biological structures[7](#CR7), but access to the brain from the periphery is restricted by the blood-brain barrier (BBB), a complex biological structure that regulates molecular access to the central nervous system (CNS)[8](#CR8)–[10](#CR10). Systemic administration of AAVs also exposes the vectors to the host immune system[11](#CR11),[12](#CR12) and off-target tissues[3](#CR3),[13](#CR13). The poor efficiency of brain targeting after systemic administration with natural serotypes often necessitates high doses that raise costs and may trigger serious adverse events[14](#CR14)–[16](#CR16). Thus, improved vectors are needed if AAV gene therapy is to realize its full therapeutic potential.

AAV capsid engineering, particularly through directed evolution methods, has demonstrated that markedly improved efficiency in desired cell types and tissues after systemic intravenous delivery is possible[17](#CR17)–[19](#CR19). In particular, two recently identified engineered capsids, AAV9-X1.1[20](#CR20) and AAV.CAP-Mac[21](#CR21), robustly transduce CNS neurons after systemic administration in macaques. As AAV capsids are applied across species, however, the enhanced tropisms of many engineered vectors can vary[20](#CR20)–[23](#CR23). This is concerning for human clinical trials, as a capsid developed in another species that performs poorly when translated to humans may not only fail to provide therapeutic benefit but might preclude future therapies for the patient by inducing neutralizing antibodies[11](#CR11).

This translational challenge of AAV engineering through directed evolution also represents an opportunity to better understand fundamental mechanisms of drug delivery to the brain. Directed evolution of engineered capsids with enhanced BBB crossing provides a platform with which researchers may survey the most efficient pathways across this barrier. While recent progress suggests that engineered AAVs may utilize diverse BBB-crossing receptors[24](#CR24)–[27](#CR27), the mechanisms of primate brain-enhanced vectors[20](#CR20),[21](#CR21),[23](#CR23),[28](#CR28)–[30](#CR30) remain underexplored.

To address this challenge, here we adapt Retrogenix cell microarrays[31](#CR31),[32](#CR32) of the human membrane proteome and secretome to screen natural and engineered AAV capsid interactions with host cells. This allows us to rapidly assay more than 90% of the known human membrane proteome and secretome, including key protein classes such as receptors, transporters, and cytokines. This unbiased screen should thus include nearly all proteins exposed to an intravenously-injected AAV prior to cell internalization. Using this broad, unbiased screen, we identify several previously-unreported AAV interactions with implications for the host immune response (human interleukin 3 (IL3) binding to AAV9), enhanced BBB crossing across species (via low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 6 (LRP6) binding by AAV9-X1.1 and AAV.CAP-Mac), and peripheral tissue tropism (through pancreas-expressed glycoprotein 2 (GP2) binding by AAV9-X1.1 and CAP-Mac). We then characterize these capsid interactions using diverse biophysical and structural methods, including cryo-electron tomography. Finally, we functionally validate LRP6 capsid interactions in vivo in mice, in the human BBB via primary cell culture, and beyond the BBB using human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived neurons. Understanding the mechanism of action of systemic AAVs through methods such as those used here will be critical for successful vector translation and should enable design of improved vectors, as well as other therapeutic protein modalities, for specific targets[33](#CR33),[34](#CR34).

## Results

### High-throughput screening for AAV binding partners

To screen AAV-binding proteins, we used Retrogenix cell microarrays[31](#CR31),[32](#CR32) of the human membrane proteome and secretome, in which DNA oligonucleotides (oligos) encoding human membrane and secreted proteins are affixed at known slide locations (Fig. [1a](#Fig1)). HEK293 cells are then grown on the slides and become individually reverse-transfected with the oligos in the corresponding pattern. AAVs that directly interact with a given protein will preferentially bind to cells expressing that protein; other slide locations define non-specific background binding. To increase confidence in binding specificity, each protein is patterned at two different locations (four locations for initial condition optimization) (Fig. [1b, c](#Fig1)). We optimized screen conditions using previously-identified AAV and interacting protein pairs, (1) AAV9 with AAVR (KIAA0319L)[35](#CR35) and (2) PHP.eB with mouse LY6A[25](#CR25)–[27](#CR27), and two different detection methods: biotin tagging and direct antibody detection (Fig. [1](#Fig1)b, [c](#Fig1)). Biotinylated capsids were detected with fluorescent streptavidin, and unlabeled capsids were detected with an antibody whose epitope is distinct from the commonly engineered capsid variable regions (VR) IV and VIII[18](#CR18),[36](#CR36). As noted previously[37](#CR37),[38](#CR38), capsid primary amine labeling levels must be tuned so that surface modification does not interfere with key capsid binding interactions. We found that the best signal to noise ratio for duplicate spots (calculated as the average intensity of positive control spots compared to the average intensity of the rest of the slide) was achieved by directly fixing cell-bound AAVs without washing.

Testing these capsids individually revealed that all except MaCPNS1 exhibited detectable AAVR binding (the exception may be due to the interfering geometry of the capsid’s VR-VIII insertion[39](#CR39)), whereas only CAP-B22 interacted with mouse LY6A (likely through the PHP.eB loop in VR-VIII[25](#CR25)–[27](#CR27)) (Fig. [1d](#Fig1) and Supplementary Fig. [1](#MOESM1)). To enable higher-throughput screening, we decided to test the six capsids as a pool. Pooled testing required additional dosage optimization, first for the individual and then for the collective background binding levels of the included capsids (Supplementary Table [1](#MOESM1)). An optimal dose was determined that minimized background binding while still allowing the specific interaction of CAP-B22 with mouse LY6A to be distinguished from the five non-LY6A-interacting capsids (Fig. [1d](#Fig1)).

After these controls, we then tested the six-capsid pool in a full screen of over 6400 proteins, including 6019 human plasma membrane proteins and secreted and cell surface-tethered proteins, as well as 397 heterodimers. This unbiased screen includes more than 90% of the human membrane proteome and secretome. We identified 22 pool hits with enhanced signal over background in each duplicate spot. To assign these hits to specific capsids in the pool, we performed follow-up deconvolution screens with each individual capsid from the pool (Fig. [1e](#Fig1)). DNA oligos for the 22 identified hits, as well as the positive control CD86 and negative control EGFR, were affixed in duplicate locations to new slides. A negative control condition with no AAV analyte and a positive control condition with CTLA4-Fc (CD86 binder) were also included. We were able to successfully assign hits, including both membrane-localized and secreted proteins, to capsids. Some of these interactions were specific to select AAV9 variants, such as LRP6 for AAV9-X1.1 or FAM234A for AAV.CAP-B22, while others were conserved across all capsids tested, such as IL3 (Table [2](#Tab2)).

### Validation of AAV binding interaction with interleukin-3

To validate binders from our cell microarray screen, membrane protein hits were tested for their ability to enhance AAV potency in cell culture (Supplementary Fig. [2](#MOESM1)) and secreted protein capsid-binding interactions, as well as soluble membrane protein extracellular domains, were characterized by surface plasmon resonance (SPR) (Fig. [2a](#Fig2), Supplementary Fig. [3](#MOESM1)). This reduced the candidate receptors to a subset of validated interactors (Table [2](#Tab2)). We were struck by the identified interaction of AAV9 and all its recent lab-evolved derivatives with the human immunomodulatory protein IL3 because AAVs are relatively well tolerated by the immune system[40](#CR40). IL3 is produced by activated T cells as part of the inflammatory response to viral infection, triggering expansion of various immune cells and activating type I interferon-secreting plasmacytoid dendritic cells[41](#CR41). Using SPR, we found that human IL3 binds AAV9 but not the closely related natural serotypes AAV8 and AAVrh10[42](#CR42) (Fig. [2b](#Fig2)). We then tested IL3 from different species, finding that AAV9 binds to human and macaque IL3 (83% amino acid \[AA\] identity) but not marmoset or mouse IL3 (69% and 27% AA identity with human, respectively) (Fig. [2c](#Fig2)), suggesting a binding site divergence between new and old world monkeys. As interaction with human IL3 was observed in the cell microarray screen for every capsid tested (Fig. [1e](#Fig1)), we also tested AAV9-X1.1 and observed binding with human but not mouse IL3 by SPR (Fig. [2d](#Fig2)). The conservation of human IL3 binding across AAV9 derivatives implies that neither substitutions at VR-IV nor insertions at VR-VIII deleteriously impact this naturally evolved interaction.

To further understand the species and serotype specificity of human IL3’s interaction with AAV9, we investigated the structure of the bound complex. As functional AAV ligands may have weak and dynamic monomeric interactions[43](#CR43), we leveraged avidity by flowing the 60-mer AAV9 capsid over protein A-captured dimeric IL3-Fc to ensure all biologically meaningful interactions are detected[24](#CR24). Despite this high avidity in the SPR experiment, the apparent affinity of the interaction was consistent with only a high nM interaction. Therefore, we began our structural studies by performing chemical cross-linking of IL3-bound AAV9, followed by tandem mass spectrometry (XL-MS/MS)[44](#CR44). Using bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (BS3) cross-linking agent, 2 high-confidence cross-links between the proteins were detected (Fig. [3a](#Fig3), Supplementary Fig. [4](#MOESM1), and Supplementary Table [2](#MOESM1)). These cross-links place IL3’s interaction site with AAV9 near the base of the threefold symmetry spike and the twofold symmetry depression, a region containing multiple residues that are specific to AAV9 compared to non-interacting serotypes (Fig. [3b](#Fig3)). We tested chimeric AAV9 capsids with each variable region individually mutated to AAV8 amino acid identity by SPR and found that human IL3 binding is most strongly determined by VR-I and VR-V (Fig. [3c](#Fig3) and Supplementary Table [3](#MOESM1)). We used a similar chimeric strategy to substitute human IL3 residues with those from marmoset, which indicated that the N-terminus of human IL3 is critical for AAV9 binding (Supplementary Fig. [5](#MOESM1)).

Next, we turned to cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), which is well suited to capturing dynamic interactions and resolving low-occupancy or heterogenous ligands on the surface of AAVs[45](#CR45),[46](#CR46). Sub-tomogram averaging of 2661 hand-picked viral particles resulted in an initial 11.0 Å resolution map of the capsid after enforcing I1 symmetry (Supplementary Fig. [6](#MOESM1)a, [b](#MOESM1) and Supplementary Table [4](#MOESM1)). While the high sigma map did not show any obvious IL3 density, adjusting the map to a low sigma suggested that such density was potentially present (Supplementary Fig. [6](#MOESM1)c, [d](#MOESM1)). To bypass confounding heterogeneity in binding site occupancy in the 60mer AAV and facilitate alignment of small ligands, we performed I1 symmetry expansion and particle subtraction around the AAV trimer (Supplementary Fig. [6](#MOESM1)a, [e](#MOESM1)). This overlaid each asymmetric component of the capsid on the same reference frame to extract the threefold symmetry face, generating 159,660 particles. After further 3D classification and refinement without imposing symmetry, this yielded a map of the AAV capsid threefold symmetry face that contains density protruding from a side of the threefold symmetry spike that cannot be explained by the AAV capsid alone (Fig. [3d](#Fig3), shown in red, and Supplementary Fig. [6f](#MOESM1)).

We performed rigid body docking of IL3 into this averaged cryo-ET density (Supplementary Fig. [7](#MOESM1)), guided by the distance constraints identified by XL-MS/MS (Supplementary Fig. [4a](#MOESM1)) and our SPR experiments showing that AAV9 VR-I and VR-V (Fig. [3c](#Fig3)) as well as the N-terminus of human IL3 (Supplementary Fig. [5](#MOESM1)) are critical for binding. Within the sub-volume average there is density that can only be explained by one bound IL3. However, the pose suggests one IL3 would not sterically hinder another IL3 binding within the same threefold face. The IL3 binding site we identify overlaps with the known binding sites for AAVR and galactose. However, given the high number of potential binding sites on the full 60-mer capsid, the physiological relevance of this binding site overlap is uncertain.

### Validation of AAV binding interaction with LRP6

We next assessed the validated AAV interactors for their potential to explain the enhanced brain tropisms of the engineered capsids. Sorting the screen hits by their expression level in endothelial cells of the human BBB[47](#CR47) spotlighted a specific interaction of LRP6 with AAV9-X1.1 (Fig. [4a](#Fig4)). This capsid displays enhanced brain endothelial-specific tropism in mice that shifts to enhanced neuronal tropism in macaque (Table [1](#Tab1))[20](#CR20). Although AAV9-X1.1 contains modifications from AAV9 at both variable regions IV and VIII (Table [1](#Tab1)), we previously showed that the tropism of AAV9-X1.1 could be transferred to other natural serotypes such as AAV1 and AAV-DJ by transferring only the VR-VIII insertion of AAV9-X1.1[20](#CR20). By SPR, here we confirm that the X1 peptide insertion in VR-VIII endows AAV1-X1 and AAVDJ-X1, but not their unmodified parent serotypes, with LRP6 binding (Supplementary Fig. [8a](#MOESM1)). This demonstrates that the functional modularity of the X1 peptide in different AAV serotypes in vivo corresponds to LRP6-binding modularity.

LRP6 is a coreceptor of the canonical Wnt signaling pathway, with developmental and homeostatic roles in many tissues[48](#CR48)–[50](#CR50). The high degree of LRP6 sequence conservation across species (98% and 99.5% AA identity between human LRP6 and mouse or macaque LRP6, respectively) aligns with AAV9-X1.1’s enhanced tropism compared to AAV9 in rodents and primates. A similar enhancement in tropism across species is also seen for CAP-Mac[21](#CR21) (Table [1](#Tab1)), which was engineered in marmosets and has enhanced endothelial tropism compared to AAV9 in marmosets as well as enhanced neuronal tropism in macaque. Therefore, we also tested CAP-Mac by SPR for interaction with the human LRP6 extracellular domain (Fig. [4b](#Fig4)). As with IL3, we utilized avidity to ensure that weak yet functionally important interactions were captured. Both AAV9-X1.1 and CAP-Mac strongly bind human LRP6-Fc, unlike their parent capsid, AAV9, with a sub-nM apparent affinity.

LRP6 has many endogenous Wnt signaling partners with binding sites spanning either extracellular YWTD domains 1 and 2 (E1E2) or domains 3 and 4 (E3E4)[51](#CR51). We applied AlphaFold-Multimer[52](#CR52) to build models of LRP6-AAV interaction complexes, which predicted that the X1 and CAP-Mac VR-VIII peptides bind LRP6 YWTD domain 1 (Fig. [4c](#Fig4)). While the cooperative folding of E1 and E2 complicates testing of individual domains[53](#CR53), SPR of mouse LRP6 extracellular domain fragments was consistent with the model predictions, with interaction observed for LRP6-E1E2 but not LRP6-E3E4 (Fig. [4d](#Fig4)). We also tested AAV-BI30, another engineered capsid with specific tropism for the mouse brain endothelium[54](#CR54) (Table [1](#Tab1)), finding that it also binds to LRP6-E1E2 but not LRP6-E3E4 (Supplementary Fig. [8b](#MOESM1)). A pull-down assay confirmed that both AAV9-X1.1 and CAP-Mac bind to AAVR’s PKD2 domain and the full length extracellular domain of mouse LRP6 but not that of closely-related LRP5 (Supplementary Fig. [9a](#MOESM1))[51](#CR51). AAV9, on the other hand, bound only to AAVR’s PKD2, as reported previously[39](#CR39). Subsequent semi-quantitative pulldown experiments suggested that the strength of CAP-Mac’s interaction with AAVR PKD2 is similar to that of AAV9 (Supplementary Fig. [9b](#MOESM1)). In contrast, AAV9-X1.1, like PHP.eB[39](#CR39), had a slightly reduced affinity for AAVR PKD2 compared to AAV9. Interaction of both engineered capsids with galactose was unaffected in pulldown experiments (Supplementary Fig. [9c](#MOESM1)).

AAV9-X1.1 and CAP-Mac potently infect HEK293 cells, with AAV9-X1.1 having a stronger effect (Supplementary Fig. [10a](#MOESM1)). To determine if this potency is mediated by endogenous LRP6 expression in HEK293 cells, we tested the effect of LRP6 inhibitors. AAV9-X1.1 potency was markedly reduced by mesoderm development LRP chaperone (Mesd), a natural endoplasmic reticulum chaperone and exogenous extracellular inhibitor of LRP5 and LRP6[55](#CR55), and sclerostin (SOST), which inhibits LRP6 through specific binding of E1E2 alone[56](#CR56) (Supplementary Fig. [10](#MOESM1)). Importantly, neither Mesd nor SOST inhibited the potency of PHP.eB in LY6A-overexpressing cells. Transient overexpression of human LRP6 boosted the potency of both AAV9-X1.1 and CAP-Mac, with a stronger effect for CAP-Mac (Supplementary Fig. [10a](#MOESM1)). This effect was largely preserved with a construct excising LRP6-E3E4. As expected from our pull-down assay, transient overexpression of LRP5 did not enhance the potency of either CAP-Mac or AAV9-X1.1. Together, these results support a specific functional interaction between LRP6 and both CAP-Mac and AAV9-X1.1, although the two capsids may have different functional sensitivities to LRP6 expression level. While AAV9-X1.1 productively engages LRP6 at the lower endogenous expression levels of LRP6 on HEK293 cells, CAP-Mac shows greater potency when LRP6 is overexpressed.

Of note, in addition to the intended CNS receptors gained through AAV capsid engineering, both LRP6-binding capsids also gained interactions with the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-linked protein glycoprotein 2 (GP2), which is expressed specifically in the pancreas and, in a secreted form, plays an antibacterial role in the gut[57](#CR57),[58](#CR58) (Supplementary Fig. [2a](#MOESM1), Supplementary Fig. [3](#MOESM1), and Table [2](#Tab2)). GP2 boosted the potency of both capsids in cell culture, with a stronger effect elicited by the human protein than the mouse (Supplementary Fig. [2a](#MOESM1)).

FAM234A, which bound CAP-B22 in the cell microarray screen, is found in the brain with weak expression in many neuron types[59](#CR59). Although FAM234A has been identified in disease-association studies[60](#CR60), no specific molecular function has been assigned. We found that FAM234A enhances the potency of both CAP-B22 and PHP.eB in cell culture, with the mouse protein showing a stronger effect than the human protein (Supplementary Fig. [2b](#MOESM1)). This suggests that the interaction is driven by these capsids’ shared VR-VIII insertion peptide (Table [1](#Tab1)).

### NHP brain-enhanced AAVs utilize LRP6 at the mouse BBB and in primate cell culture

Host neutralizing antibodies, developed in response to prior exposure to AAVs, complicate repeat administration with the same serotype. Serotype-switched X1 vectors, such as AAV1-X1, were shown to enable a second systemic dosing in mice previously exposed to AAV9-based vectors[20](#CR20). We leveraged this property to determine the in vivo effects of AAV9-X1.1’s LRP6 interaction (Fig. [5a](#Fig5)). Brain endothelium-targeted AAV1-X1 packaging either control mCherry or Cre recombinase was systemically administered to *Lrp6* Cre-conditional knockout mice. After three weeks, either AAV9-based PHP.eB or AAV9-X1.1 packaging eGFP was systemically delivered. ## Discussion

Recent advances in capsid engineering have led to AAV vectors that can more efficiently cross the BBB in rodents and NHPs after systemic administration[17](#CR17)–[19](#CR19), but predictable translation and further rational design of these and other, non-viral BBB-crossing molecules is hampered by our limited understanding of transcytosis mechanisms, particularly in humans. This translational challenge is also an opportunity to better understand the biology of the BBB and AAV vectors. To date, only a few targets, such as transferrin receptor (TfR)[62](#CR62), have been used for research or therapies. Here, we developed a pipeline to find cognate receptors for engineered AAVs, focusing on the human membrane proteome and secretome. Our results validate the utility of cell microarray screening to identify receptors for natural and engineered AAVs. We identify LRP6 as a previously-unreported and highly-conserved target for BBB transcytosis by AAV9-X1.1, a potent engineered capsid for primate CNS neurons after intravenous injection[20](#CR20) and human IL3 as an interaction partner for AAV9. These findings offer the prospect of leveraging identified receptors for targeted drug delivery across diverse therapeutic modalities, such as small molecules, antibodies, or oligonucleotides.

## Abstract

Broadening gene therapy applications requires manufacturable vectors that efficiently transduce target cells in humans and preclinical models. Conventional selections of adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid libraries are inefficient at searching the vast sequence space for the small fraction of vectors possessing multiple traits essential for clinical translation. Here, we present Fit4Function, a generalizable machine learning (ML) approach for systematically engineering multi-trait AAV capsids. By leveraging a capsid library that uniformly samples the manufacturable sequence space, reproducible screening data are generated to train accurate sequence-to-function models. Combining six models, we designed a multi-trait (liver-targeted, manufacturable) capsid library and validated 88% of library variants on all six predetermined criteria. Furthermore, the models, trained only on mouse in vivo and human in vitro Fit4Function data, accurately predicted AAV capsid variant biodistribution in macaque. Top candidates exhibited production yields comparable to AAV9, efficient murine liver transduction, up to 1000-fold greater human hepatocyte transduction, and increased enrichment relative to AAV9 in a screen for liver transduction in macaques. The Fit4Function strategy ultimately makes it possible to predict cross-species traits of peptide-modified AAV capsids and is a critical step toward assembling an ML atlas that predicts AAV capsid performance across dozens of traits.

However, variants optimized for one trait may be difficult to co-optimize for other traits, and the protein sequence space is too vast to effectively sample by chance for rare variants that are enhanced across multiple traits. As a result, AAV engineering teams often devote many years and significant resources to developing capsids that ultimately fail to be optimized across multiple traits essential for preclinical and clinical translation.

To identify novel and diverse AAV capsids that simultaneously possess multiple traits relevant to gene delivery (e.g., manufacturability, targeting to disease-relevant cells across host species, detargeting from other cell types), vast capsid sequence spaces must be subjected to systematic and unbiased searches. This quickly becomes intractable using traditional methods as the capsid sequence is increasingly modified. For instance, merely inserting a string of seven amino acids (a 7-mer) into an AAV9 capsid generates a theoretical sequence space of 1.28 billion variants; inserting a 10-mer instead of a 7-mer extends that space to 10 trillion variants.

To address this challenge, we sought to develop a generalizable ML-guided approach to systematically and simultaneously map 7-mer-modified AAV9 capsid sequences to multiple traits of interest. To generate high-quality data that would enable the training of accurate ML models, it was necessary to first create a low-bias, high-diversity library composed only of “production-fit” capsid variants that are capable of assembling and packaging a genome (Fig. [1](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig1)). This “Fit4Function” library was subjected to in vivo and in vitro screens for traits relevant to gene therapy, which, as anticipated, resulted in highly reproducible data that could be used to train robust ML models. The models trained using the Fit4Function data were of sufficient accuracy that they could be leveraged in combination to search the much larger, untested, theoretical production-fit sequence space in silico for rare multi-trait variants. We first demonstrated that six models relating to production fitness and liver-targeting in vitro and in vivo could be used in combination to predict sequences that met filters set across all six models. The resulting library of variants exhibited a high 88.4% validation rate, i.e., 88.4% of its variants were experimentally determined to fulfill all six criteria. Despite being trained only on mouse in vivo and human in vitro data, this combination of six models translated to the macaque. Variants nominated for individual validation performed well across human cells and mice compared to AAV9. These same variants provided more efficient transduction of the macaque liver relative to AAV9 when tested in a pooled library format. Notably, the combination of in vivo and in vitro functional predictors boosted the precision of cross-species prediction compared to the use of any individual model. In other words, although it has been argued that human cell models are less useful than animal models in AAV gene delivery vector development, we observed that models trained on data from human cell in vitro functional assays were valuable for predicting variants that exhibit the trait of interest in mice and macaques in vivo. The Fit4Function approach allowed us to systematically identify the combination of traits that is most critical in predicting a given function of interest; appropriate screening models can be identified and used to enrich for multi-trait capsids. This strategy can inform intelligent searches for AAV capsids that are performant across species and more likely to translate from preclinical models to investigational human gene therapies.

## Results

### Production fitness sequence space mapping

We and others have successfully derived enhanced gene delivery vectors from AAV9 capsids modified through the insertion of seven amino acids (7-mer) between VP1 residues 588–589. To create an accurate and generalizable sequence-to-production-fitness ML model, synthetic modeling and assessment libraries were designed for the purposes of training and validating the model, respectively. Each consists of 74.5K variants that uniformly sample the sequence space (each amino acid was sampled with an equal probability at each position); 10K of the 74.5K are common to both libraries to assess reproducibility across libraries. This is distinct from conventional NNN or NNK (where N is any base and K is a G or T) libraries where millions of variants are synthesized stochastically by uniformly sampling the nucleotide space, which biases toward amino acids represented by more codons. Both modeling and assessment libraries were also designed to assess whether codon usage impacts production fitness; each variant is represented by two maximally different nucleotide sequences (codon replicates, i.e., replicates that encode the same seven amino acid residues but using different codons to serve as in-sample biological replicates). We produced both libraries in triplicate, in two separate runs, by two different researchers, for a total of twelve replicates each. The reproducibility (measured by the agreement between replicates) of variant production fitness scores between preparations by different researchers improved as technical, codon, and biological replicates were aggregated (Supplementary Fig. [1](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#MOESM1)). Therefore, we performed all subsequent analyses on production fitness scores aggregated across all replicates for each library.

We first assessed whether codon usage impacts the production fitness of identical amino acid variants. If so, it would be necessary to train on the nucleotide sequence space (617 for NNN, 317 for NNK), which is much larger than the amino acid sequence space (207). We observed a high correlation between the production fitness scores of the codon replicates in the modeling library (Fig. [2a](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2) and Supplementary Fig. [2](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#MOESM1)), suggesting no significant codon usage bias. Therefore, we averaged production fitness across codon replicates for all downstream modeling.

The production fitness distribution of the modeling library could be modeled by a mixture of two Gaussian distributions: a “non-fit” versus a “production-fit” distribution (Fig. [2b](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)). Note that the “production-fit” distribution includes variants that produce better than, as well as, or less well than AAV9; “production-fit” is not defined as having a production fitness score greater than that of AAV9. The non-fit distribution overlaps with the production fitness distribution of the stop-codon-containing variants, which are presumably detected at low levels in the AAV library due to cross-packaging (Supplementary Fig. [3](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#MOESM1)). The variants in the production-fit distribution exhibit distinguishing amino acid sequence characteristics such as a general enrichment of negatively charged residues and the depletion of cysteine and tryptophan (Fig. [2c](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)). Nonetheless, this production-fit distribution had less bias than an analogous set of the most abundant 74.5K variants from an NNK library (Fig. [2c](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)). The production fitness scores for the 10K variants common to both libraries were consistent (Fig. [2d](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)), suggesting that variant fitness is not noticeably impacted by the other variants in each of the libraries.

### A generalizable production fitness model

While prior studies applied classification models to predict AAV capsid production fitness[13](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR13 "Bryant, D. H. et al. Deep diversification of an AAV capsid protein by machine learning. Nat. Biotechnol. 39, 691–696 (2021)."),[14](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR14 "Marques, A. D. et al. Applying machine learning to predict viral assembly for adeno-associated virus capsid libraries. Mol. Ther. Methods Clin. Dev. 20, 276–286 (2021)."), we used a regression model to capture the large variation in relative production fitness scores (±5-fold, log2 enrichment) within the production-fit and non-fit distributions. We first trained the model using the sequence and production fitness measurements of 24K variants unique to the modeling library. The accuracy of each model in this study was assessed by the agreement (Pearson correlation) between the measured fitness scores and the model’s predicted scores. Remarkably, the sequence-to-production-fitness model achieved high accuracy on the remaining subset of the modeling library not used in the training process (Fig. [2e](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)), as well as the independent assessment library (Fig. [2f](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)). In addition, the model does not require large amounts of training data to obtain high accuracy, reducing the training from 24K to 5K variants only slightly reduced performance (*r* = 0.924 ± 0.001 vs *r* = 0.899 ± 0.015, Fig. [2g](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig2)). These data demonstrate that the model is generalizable across libraries and to unseen variants and requires relatively small training datasets given the high quality of the data.

### Fit4Function enables reproducible data and accurate prediction models

Using the production fitness model, we randomly generated and predicted the fitness of 24M variants in silico. The predicted production-fit sequence space was then uniformly sampled for 240K variants to create a “Fit4Function” library. As expected, the measured fitness scores for the Fit4Function variants, when synthesized, mapped to a single distribution that closely follows the production-fit distribution of the modeling library (Fig. [3a](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3)). The amino acid distribution in the Fit4Function library is similar to that of the production-fit distribution from the modeling library and is similarly less biased when compared to that of the 240K most abundant variants in an NNK library (Fig. [3b](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3)). It is important to note that the production-fit threshold used in populating Fit4Function libraries is not so stringent as to eliminate potentially promising functional candidates for downstream optimization; only non-fit variants with poor production (those whose production fitness is comparable to stop-codon-containing control sequences) are not sampled for Fit4Function libraries. Nonetheless, the Fit4Function approach enables users to set their own fitness thresholds, e.g., one could require that the majority of the capsid variants in their library produce at least as well as AAV9.

Fit4Function libraries are designed to enable the generation of reproducible and ML-compatible functional screening data. Specifically, the library is limited to a moderate size that enables deeper sequencing depth and samples only production-fit variants, which both enable more quantitative and reliable detection of each variant in the library. In addition, the library samples the production-fit amino acid sequence space in an even manner, which results in less biased and more generalizable ML models.

To demonstrate the high-quality, ML-compatible screening data enabled by the Fit4Function approach, we first compared the outcomes of our screening strategy using the Fit4Function library versus an NNK library across five functional assays: (1) HEK293 cell binding, (2) primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cell (BMVEC) binding, (3) primary human BMVEC binding, (4) human brain endothelial cell line (hCMEC/D3) binding, and (5) HEK293 transduction. Binding and transduction were measured by quantitative sequencing capsid variant abundance at the DNA and mRNA levels, respectively. The Fit4Function library consistently yielded higher replication quality data than the NNK library (one-tailed paired *t*\-test, *n* = 5 assays; *p* = 0.0065; Fig. [3c](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3)).

Second, we built and compared models trained on functional data derived from the Fit4Function library versus an NNK library (only data from the most abundant 240K variants in the NNK AAV library were used). The Fit4Function-based models consistently achieved higher prediction accuracy (Fig. [3d](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3)). These results are unsurprising because NNK libraries have theoretically millions of random variants, some of which can be at levels that are two or more orders of magnitude higher than other variants in the library. As a result, state-of-the-art sequencing is not able to accurately quantify a great number of the underrepresented variants in NNK libraries before and after screens. In addition, the unknown variant membership in NNK libraries and the resulting low-quality data mean that ML models cannot be trained to discriminate between truly non-functional variants and variants that cannot be reliably detected. In comparison, Fit4Function libraries that are sized at 240K variants or less have a manageable, known membership and focus on production-fit variants, which increases the likelihood of detection for each variant. Critically, this allows for accurate functional learning and predictions from both positive and negative data. Furthermore, Fit4Function libraries used for training functional fitness models are populated with variants sampled uniformly across the sequence space. Compared to NNK libraries, the higher replication quality and reduced bias in Fit4Function libraries enable more accurate modeling.

We next sought to examine the use of the Fit4Function library to train prediction models for more complex functions where NNK screening data would typically be sparse and challenging to use for training accurate models. Here we considered in vivo AAV biodistribution after systemic administration in four adult C57BL/6J mice. The replication quality was high in the liver, kidney, and spleen, and moderate in the brain, spinal cord, heart, lungs, and in serum (Fig. [3e](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3) and Supplementary Fig. [4](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#MOESM1)). We trained independent models to predict the variant tropism for each organ. The training data measurements were aggregated across three animals, and the data from the fourth animal was held out for independent testing. The models performed reasonably well when trained on assays with more reproducible data (Fig. [3f](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3); model performance correlated with the data replication quality shown in Fig. [3e](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig3)), demonstrating the applicability of our approach to in vivo data.

### Multi-trait capsid identification

Efficient and durable gene delivery to the liver remains challenging due to vector efficiency, capsid antigen presentation, and T cell-mediated immunity. Liver-directed therapies should benefit from the development of more potent AAV vectors that can be administered at lower doses to reduce exposure to capsid antigens. Previous efforts to develop capsids with improved human hepatocyte transduction have generated candidates that are selective for human hepatocytes but inefficiently transduce the mouse liver in vivo[2](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR2 "Lisowski, L. et al. Selection and evaluation of clinically relevant AAV variants in a xenograft liver model. Nature 506, 382–386 (2014)."),[15](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR15 "Qian, R., Xiao, B., Li, J. & Xiao, X. Directed evolution of AAV serotype 5 for increased hepatocyte transduction and retained low humoral seroreactivity. Mol. Ther. Methods Clin. Dev. 20, 122–132 (2021)."). While such vectors have important translational potential—one capsid, LK03 is now being evaluated in human clinical trials (NCT05092685; NCT04581785; NCT03003533; NCT03876301)[2](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR2 "Lisowski, L. et al. Selection and evaluation of clinically relevant AAV variants in a xenograft liver model. Nature 506, 382–386 (2014).")—there is a need for capsids that exhibit improved tropisms across species so that they are also compatible with preclinical efficacy and safety testing.

Our objective was to design a MultiFunction library consisting only of variants that are each predicted to possess multiple enhanced functions related to cross-species hepatocyte gene delivery. Notably, AAV9 has a strong liver transduction profile in animals compared to other AAV serotypes, including AAV5 and AAV8[16](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#ref-CR16 "Zincarelli, C., Soltys, S., Rengo, G. & Rabinowitz, J. E. Analysis of AAV serotypes 1–9 mediated gene expression and tropism in mice after systemic injection. Mol. Ther. 16, 1073–1080 (2008)."). Therefore, an AAV9-based capsid engineered to efficiently target the liver across species could be a candidate for a liver gene therapy vector. We performed five separate functional screens of the Fit4Function library: (1) binding or (2) transduction of the human hepatocellular carcinoma cell line (HEPG2), (3) binding or (4) transduction of the human liver epithelial cell line (THLE-2), and (5) efficient liver biodistribution in C57BL/6J mice (Supplementary Fig. [5](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#MOESM1)). We used the high-quality data from these functional screens to train and assess the performance of five independent sequence-to-function models (Fig. [4a](/articles/s41467-024-50555-y#Fig4)). With the production fitness model and these five functional fitness models, we screened 10M randomly generated variants in silico and selected 30K liver-targeted MultiFunction variants predicted to have enhanced phenotypes across all five functions and production fitness (an “enhanced phenotype” was arbitrarily defined as any variant above the 50th percentile of the measured enrichment scores). In the MultiFunction library, each variant was encoded by two nucleotide sequences serving as codon replicates. In addition, we included 3K variants from the modeling library (production-fit and non-fit; Uniform Control), 10K from the Fit4Function library (Fit4Function Control), and 3K from the known hits in the Fit4Function library, i.e., variants from the Fit4Function library that had been experimentally confirmed to exhibit enhanced phenotypes for the five hepatocyte-related traits and production fitness (Positive Control).
